editorial:
The Last Command is a 1928 Paramount Famous Lasky Corp. silent film directed by Josef von Sternberg, in which Emil Jannings plays Grand Duke Sergius Alexander â€” a Russian Imperial general who survives the Bolshevik Revolution only to wash up as a destitute Hollywood extra, cast to re-enact the very battle that destroyed him. Jannings won the first Academy Award for Best Actor in part for this performance, and the film received a Best Original Story nomination at the inaugural 1929 ceremony. Paramount registered the copyright in 1928, based on an original story by Lajos BÃ­rÃ³ and von Sternberg with screenplay by John F. Goodrich, and duly renewed it â€” but the 95-year maximum term under 17 U.S.C. Â§ 304(b) ran out on January 1, 2024, placing the story, screenplay, and filmed images unambiguously in the public domain.

The one rights trap is the restoration layer. The Criterion Collection issued a DVD in 2010 ('3 Silent Classics by Josef von Sternberg,' spine 530) and Kino Lorber has distributed the film commercially as well; both releases carry a separately copyrighted video transfer and a newly commissioned musical score that did not expire with the underlying 1928 print. At least one 1080p Blu-ray rip sourced from these commercial releases is indexed on Archive.org and circulates widely â€” using it would mean reproducing the restoration's protected elements alongside the PD images. Creators should source from the Archive.org item uploaded by the official Archive.org archiver (identifier: the-last-command_1928), whose provenance predates the commercial restoration era.
faq: The film's copyright expired in 2024 â€” can I use any copy I find online?

You can freely use the underlying 1928 film, but not every copy online is clean. The Criterion Collection's 2010 DVD ('3 Silent Classics by Josef von Sternberg,' spine 530) and Kino Lorber's commercial releases carry independently copyrighted video transfers and scores. At least one 1080p Blu-ray rip of those releases is indexed on Archive.org. Use the Archive.org item the-last-command_1928, uploaded by the official Archive.org archiver, rather than a rip sourced from a commercial Blu-ray.
Can I compose my own score and release this film commercially?

Yes. The 1928 silent images are public domain and you may compose, commission, or license any musical accompaniment and sync it to the film for commercial or noncommercial release. Your new score becomes your own copyrighted work. Do not copy or directly incorporate the score from the Criterion or Kino Lorber editions, which are independently copyrighted compositions.
